theory.title: Load Balancing: Sharing the Work
theory.plainObjective: Three backends are ahead. Two have failed. Find the healthy one and deliver your packet.
theory.summary: Every major website you use - GitHub, YouTube, freeCodeCamp - runs behind a load balancer. The pattern of routing around failures is what keeps services online even when individual servers crash.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Why not just one server?
bodyParagraphs.text: A single server is a single point of failure. If it crashes, every user is affected. It also has fixed capacity - once overloaded, requests slow down or fail. Adding more servers and distributing traffic across them solves both problems at once.

bodyParagraphs.heading: What a load balancer does
bodyParagraphs.text: A load balancer sits in front of a pool of backend servers. Every incoming request goes to the load balancer, which forwards it to one backend. Clients connect to the load balancer's address, not to any server directly. The entire pool appears as a single address.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Health checks
bodyParagraphs.text: Load balancers continuously test each backend - usually a small HTTP request every few seconds. A backend that fails the check is removed from rotation until it recovers. Without health checks, the load balancer would keep sending traffic to a crashed server and requests would fail silently.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Types of failure
bodyParagraphs.text: Backends fail in different ways. A link failure (broken cable, network outage) means packets never arrive. An application failure (crashed process, full disk) means the link works but the server rejects connections. A good load balancer detects and handles both.

theory.mission: Three backends are ahead. One has a broken link, one is rejecting all connections. Find the healthy backend and deliver your packet.

termIntroductions.headline: Load Balancer
termIntroductions.body: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend servers. Clients connect to its address, not to individual backends. This improves availability and lets the backend pool scale without clients knowing anything changed.

termIntroductions.headline: Application Failure
termIntroductions.body: The link to this backend is up - packets arrive - but the application is not responding. It could be a crashed process, an out-of-memory server, or a misconfiguration. A load balancer's health check would flag this backend as unhealthy and stop sending it traffic.

termIntroductions.headline: Link Failure
termIntroductions.body: This backend is unreachable because the network link itself is broken - packets disappear before arriving. This is different from an application failure: the server might be running fine, but nothing gets through. Health checks detect link failures too.
